How to read this document

Section 1 proves the support criteria and compares them with the literature. Sections 5–8 develop the finite arithmetic used in the rational-membership tests. Sections 9–12 distinguish the hypotheses of conditional implications from the finite evidence for them. Section 13 proves the arithmetic-sampling counterexample cited in the short paper. The global notation below is supplemented by definitions where each specialised recurrence is used.

A sufficient condition need not be necessary; an equivalent condition does not prove either side. Counterexamples concern the specified estimate, and a finite computation establishes only its stated range.

The short source tags distinguish the kind of evidence being cited. [Lean] identifies a cited formal-source declaration at the specified revision and follows the status recorded in the supplied material. The four support endpoints cited in Part I were replayed with their dependency closure under Lean 4.29.1 at public commit 065e09523286; their axiom audit reports only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Other supplied files retain their individually stated status. [Cert] identifies a reported exact finite computation. [Math] identifies an ordinary argument, without asserting that no formal counterpart exists. [Cited] refers to the literature, and [Open] marks an assumption or conclusion not proved here. A statement may carry more than one tag. Parameter ranges are stated separately: a result at specified values or below a bound is not a result at arbitrarily large values.

The source links are for checking precise definitions and proof terms. They are not additional hypotheses and do not replace an explanation of the mathematics. No independent verification of every other proof is claimed. Neither the universal problem nor either rational-target question is resolved in this paper.

I. Support theorems and their proofs

Support criteria and their proofs

Reciprocal-summable supports

For every infinite set AA of positive integers with ∑a∈A1/a<∞\sum_{a\in A}1/a<\infty, the series XA(b)=∑a∈A1ba−1X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{b^a-1} is irrational at every integer base b≥2b\ge2. The proof below is ordinary mathematics and is the proof of the short paper’s Theorem 1.2. Erdős’s 1968 paper, p. 222 proves the pairwise-coprime case at every integer base and states the removal of coprimality without printing the details. The proof below gives the stated extension by averaging; no comparison with the omitted proof is possible. The linked pairwise-coprime theorem retains that extra hypothesis. The same paper says that ∑1/ni<∞\sum1/n_i<\infty could be replaced by a weaker but more complicated condition (p. 222), and suggests that for pairwise coprime supports Brun’s method could probably replace it by ∑ni<x1/ni=o(log⁡log⁡x)\sum_{n_i<x}1/n_i=o(\log\log x) (p. 226). Theorem 1.1 below proves irrationality under one explicit weaker condition without coprimality; no identification with his suggestions is asserted.

The mechanism is to make positive displacements arbitrarily small. For N>0N>0, write N=qaa+raN=q_a a+r_a, 0≤ra<a0\le r_a<a. The identity bN−1ba−1=bra∑j=0qa−1bja+bra−1ba−1\frac{b^N-1}{b^a-1} =b^{r_a}\sum_{j=0}^{q_a-1}b^{ja} +\frac{b^{r_a}-1}{b^a-1} shows that Δb,A(N):=∑a∈AbNmod⁡a−1ba−1=(bN−1)XA(b)−JN,JN∈ℤ.\Delta_{b,A}(N):=\sum_{a\in A}\frac{b^{N\operatorname{mod} a}-1}{b^a-1} =(b^N-1)X_A(b)-J_N,\qquad J_N\in\mathbb Z. The integer sum is finite, since qa=0q_a=0 for a>Na>N. Every summand of Δb,A(N)\Delta_{b,A}(N) is nonnegative and an exponent a>Na>N makes it positive. Thus XA(b)=p/qX_A(b)=p/q would imply Δb,A(N)≥1/q\Delta_{b,A}(N)\ge1/q for every N>0N>0.

Put wb,d(N)=bNmod⁡d/(bd−1)w_{b,d}(N)=b^{N\operatorname{mod} d}/(b^d-1). For a fixed positive modulus QQ and g=(Q,d)g=(Q,d), the orbit of Qmmod⁡dQm\operatorname{mod} d has length d/gd/g. The important interchange is with the infinite support. The order of the two limits matters: the observation length increases with QtQ_t fixed before tt increases. No independence of different divisibility events is assumed. The mechanism also has a definite limit. At base two and full support, the contribution of exponents a>Na>N alone gives Δ2,ℕ>0(N)>1−2−N≥1/2\Delta_{2,\mathbb N_{>0}}(N)>1-2^{-N}\ge1/2. Full-support irrationality therefore uses a different argument; its checked form appears below.

A weighted condition on the support

The reciprocal-summable case is a useful model, but powers of a fixed prime can make an exponent cheaper than its reciprocal suggests. For example, with a=2kma=2^km and mm odd, the weight below becomes 1/[m(b2k−1)]1/[m(b^{2^k}-1)]. The exponential denominator permits a large collection of odd factors at large kk.

Theorem 1.1 (A weighted summability criterion). Let b≥2b\ge2 be an integer, let 𝒫\mathcal P be a finite nonempty set of primes, and let A⊆ℕ>0A\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0} be infinite. Write h(a)=∏p∈𝒫pvp(a),h(a)=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{v_p(a)}, where vp(a)v_p(a) is the exponent of pp in aa; thus h(a)h(a) is the 𝒫\mathcal P-part of aa. If Wb,𝒫(A):=∑a∈Ah(a)a(bh(a)−1)<∞,\begin{equation} \label{eq:257-weighted-mass} W_{b,\mathcal P}(A):= \sum_{a\in A}\frac{h(a)}{a\bigl(b^{h(a)}-1\bigr)}<\infty, \end{equation} then XA(b)=∑a∈A1ba−1X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{b^a-1} is irrational. More precisely, for Δb,A(m)=∑a∈Abmmod⁡a−1ba−1,\Delta_{b,A}(m)= \sum_{a\in A}\frac{b^{m\operatorname{mod} a}-1}{b^a-1}, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 and every NN there is an m≥Nm\ge N with 0<Δb,A(m)<ε0<\Delta_{b,A}(m)<\varepsilon.

Examples and limits of the hypothesis.

Squares, powers of two and factorials satisfy reciprocal summability and therefore satisfy the base-two weighted condition. Full support does not: for any fixed finite prime set PP, its subset coprime to ∏p∈Pp\prod_{p\in P}p has weight 1/[a(b−1)]1/[a(b-1)] and divergent reciprocal sum. The set of all odd exponents also fails, by restricting to integers coprime to 2∏p∈Pp2\prod_{p\in P}p. Inclusion–exclusion in the harmonic sum proves both divergences. This is a limitation of the sufficient condition, not an argument for rationality; full support is already known to be irrational.

Writing a=hma=hm with hh its 𝒫\mathcal P-part gives the exact decomposition Wb,𝒫(A)=∑h∈ℋ𝒫1bh−1∑m≥1,hm∈A(m,∏p∈𝒫p)=11m,W_{b,\mathcal P}(A)=\sum_{h\in\mathcal H_{\mathcal P}}\frac1{b^h-1} \sum_{\substack{m\ge1,\ hm\in A\\(m,\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p)=1}}\frac1m, where ℋ𝒫\mathcal H_{\mathcal P} consists of 11 and the positive integers with no prime factor outside 𝒫\mathcal P. Each inner reciprocal sum must be finite; the displayed outer sum imposes the additional summability across different 𝒫\mathcal P-parts. For example, at base two with 𝒫={2}\mathcal P=\{2\}, choose in each layer 2k2^k, k≥1k\ge1, a finite set of odd factors whose reciprocal sum is at least 22k2^{2^k}. Every inner sum is finite, but the outer weighted sum diverges. Such finite sets exist by divergence of the harmonic sum over odd integers. Prime support also fails this criterion for every finite 𝒫\mathcal P: its contribution from primes outside 𝒫\mathcal P is a constant multiple of their divergent reciprocal sum. These failures concern the sufficient hypothesis, not rationality of the resulting values. The following construction shows, nonetheless, that this condition is strictly weaker than reciprocal summability. At base two take A⋆={2km:k≥1,m odd,m≤22k}.A_\star=\{2^k m:k\ge1,\ m\text{ odd},\ m\le2^{2^k}\}. Write HN=∑m=1N1/mH_N=\sum_{m=1}^N1/m and Nk=22kN_k=2^{2^k}. The reciprocal mass of the kkth layer is ρk=2−k∑m≤Nkm odd1m=2−k(HNk−12HNk/2)→log⁡22.\rho_k=2^{-k}\!\sum_{\substack{m\le N_k\\m\text{ odd}}}\frac1m =2^{-k}\bigl(H_{N_k}-\tfrac12H_{N_k/2}\bigr) \longrightarrow\frac{\log2}{2}. Thus ∑a∈A⋆1/a\sum_{a\in A_\star}1/a diverges. For 𝒫={2}\mathcal P=\{2\}, the weighted contribution of the same layer is 2k22k−1ρk.\frac{2^k}{2^{2^k}-1}\rho_k. Since HN≤1+log⁡NH_N\le1+\log N, these terms are at most (1+2klog⁡2)21−2k(1+2^k\log2)2^{1-2^k}, which is summable. The theorem therefore proves irrationality at every integer base for every infinite subset of this set, although its reciprocal sum diverges.

Since bh(a)−1≥2h(a)−1b^{h(a)}-1\ge2^{h(a)}-1 for every b≥2b\ge2, one has Wb,𝒫(A)≤W2,𝒫(A)W_{b,\mathcal P}(A)\le W_{2,\mathcal P}(A). Thus the base-two weighted hypothesis gives the conclusion simultaneously at every integer base. The hypothesis is also hereditary under passage to infinite subsets.

Averaging antecedents.

Both averaging proofs in this section end by choosing a term no larger than a finite mean. Duverney and Tachiya choose their index in the same way in their refinement of the Chowla–Erdős method: they average a local coefficient mass over an arithmetic progression built by the Chinese remainder theorem, and a term attaining the minimum supplies the bounds that control the tail beyond it (Section 2, (2.3)–(2.9), pp. 5–6 of the author preprint). Kaneko, Suzuki and Tachiya measure the average decay of scaled tails by Rc(q,x,z)R_c(q,x,z), their (1.7) on p. 3 of arXiv v1. Under a counting condition on the support and a bound on RcR_c, most scaled tails in a range are small, and arbitrarily small nonzero scaled tails give irrationality (Lemmas 1 and 2, pp. 6–8). The divisor-incidence coefficients #{a∈A:a∣n}\#\{a\in A:a\mid n\} are positive on every multiple of min⁡A\min A. For any splitting into two sequences the two coefficient supports therefore cover a set of positive lower density, which is incompatible with the support-counting conditions [5] requiring both counts to be o(xn/zn)o(x_n/z_n) with zn≥1z_n\ge1. Their remote-tail quantity Rc(q,x,z)R_c(q,x,z) sums only offsets j≥zj\ge z, whereas the full scaled tail ∑r≥1#{a∈A:a∣m+r}br=∑a∈Aϕa(m)=XA(b)+Δb,A(m)\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\#\{a\in A:a\mid m+r\}}{b^r} =\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(m)=X_A(b)+\Delta_{b,A}(m) is at least XA(b)X_A(b), which gives no lower bound for RcR_c. The proofs above average the displacement instead, along multiples of a modulus that freezes a finite part of AA; the weighted proof adds the dyadic average [eq:257-weighted-dyadic-average]. [Cited]

Evidence boundary.

The exact interface of Theorem 1.1, including its fixed-base conclusion and hereditary all-base clause, is kernel-checked as divisibilityWeightedClaim. Its public dependency closure was replayed under Lean 4.29.1. This does not cover all infinite supports, supply a quantitative irrationality measure, or assert theorem priority.

Formalisation coverage and remaining dependencies

Every theorem, lemma, proposition and corollary of this record has a Lean statement of the same assertion, with the same hypotheses, checked by the Lean kernel using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, in the development at revision 181078b6b009. The snapshot link in the paragraph above identifies an earlier published checkpoint; the coverage statement here is about the development revision just named. Statements the record takes from the literature are attributed where they appear, and the [Cited] tag marks a clause that invokes an external result. Theorem 6.20 is attributed in this way to the periodic-weight irrationality theorem of Luca and Tachiya . No formal proof of their theorem is given here; Theorem 6.20 and the support statements following from it each carry a separate formal proof of their own assertion.

Theorem 1.2 (A summable family of divisor majorants). For each j≥1j\ge1, let Fj⊆ℕ>0F_j\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{>0} be finite, let 0<αj≤10<\alpha_j\le1, and let cj,d≥0c_{j,d}\ge0 satisfy fFj(n)αj≤∑d∣ncj,d(n≥1).f_{F_j}(n)^{\alpha_j}\le\sum_{d\mid n}c_{j,d}\quad(n\ge1). Every finite set admits such a majorant: take αj=1\alpha_j=1 and cj,d=𝟏Fj(d)c_{j,d}=\mathbf1_{F_j}(d). The restrictive part is summability over the whole family, not the existence of a majorant for an individual set. For example, Fj={4j}F_j=\{4^j\} with these choices contributes 2−j2^{-j} to [eq:257-strengthened-cover], so the theorem applies. Full support cannot admit a cover satisfying the theorem, because the proof gives arbitrarily small positive displacements and the full-support displacement is at least 1/21/2.

Combining the two support criteria

Separate small-displacement witnesses need not occur at the same index. For example, a sequence small only at even indices and one small only at odd indices need never have a small sum. The useful feature of [eq:257-mixed-finite-kernel] is its uniformity in the moving modulus: the positive-cover argument can use the exact observation window selected by the weighted proof.

Theorem 1.3 (mixed weighted and cover supports). Let E,V⊆ℕ>0E,V\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{>0}. Suppose EE has finite weighted mass [eq:257-weighted-mass] at b=2b=2 for a finite nonempty prime set 𝒫\mathcal P. Suppose also that V⊆⋃jFjV\subseteq\bigcup_jF_j for sets and majorants satisfying Theorem 1.2, with [eq:257-strengthened-cover] or its positive-weight variant. Then XA(b)X_A(b) is irrational for every infinite A⊆E∪VA\subseteq E\cup V and every integer b≥2b\ge2.

Lean: mixedSupportClaim, arbitraryWeightMixedSupport_allBase_hereditary.

The finite estimate [eq:257-weighted-final-diagonal], with complementary weighted mass κ\kappa, remains valid for this LL: its proof requires only that every member of FF divide LL. It also applies to finite or empty EE, since positivity was used only after the averaging estimate. Thus 𝒟Q;M,M(Δ2,E/ρ)<18\mathscr D_{Q;M,M}(\Delta_{2,E}/\rho)<\frac18 for sufficiently large HH. For the same finite distribution, [eq:257-mixed-finite-kernel] and nonnegative interchange give 𝒟Q;M,MSJ≤(1+4Q/M)KJ<18,SJ=∑j>Jtj−αjVj,\mathscr D_{Q;M,M}S_J\le(1+4Q/M)K_J<\frac18, \qquad S_J=\sum_{j>J}t_j^{-\alpha_j}V_j, because Q/M→0Q/M\to0. Hence some sample N=QmN=Qm satisfies Δ2,E(N)/ρ+SJ(N)<1\Delta_{2,E}(N)/\rho+S_J(N)<1. At this index the weighted displacement is below ρ\rho and Uj(N)<tjU_j(N)<t_j for every j>Jj>J. The earlier terms vanish because every exponent in their finite sets divides LL, and hence divides NN. Therefore Δ2,A(N)≤Δ2,E(N)+Δ2,V(N)<2ρ<ε,N≥Q≥L≥N0.\Delta_{2,A}(N)\le\Delta_{2,E}(N)+\Delta_{2,V}(N)<2\rho<\varepsilon, \qquad N\ge Q\ge L\ge N_0. Overlaps between the supports only improve the inequality. Infinitude of AA makes its displacement positive. The atom comparison used in the cover proof transfers arbitrarily small displacements to every integer base; the fixed rational lattice then excludes rationality. ◻

The strengthened cover conclusion is kernel-checked as strengthenedPositiveCoverClaim, and the common-witness conclusion is kernel-checked as mixedSupportClaim. Their public dependency closure was replayed under Lean 4.29.1. The arbitrary-positive-weight cover and mixed-support conclusions are also kernel-checked as arbitraryWeightPositiveCover_allBase_hereditary and arbitraryWeightMixedSupport_allBase_hereditary; the latter gives the theorem’s hereditary all-base conclusion for the arbitrary-weight branch. This theorem does not establish strict enlargement over both individual classes. The weighted non-cover host has a separate source body in the weighted support without a strengthened cover; the proposed cover-only host is not established here. It also leaves universal irrationality and the quantitative and prime-power thinning claims open here. [Math]

With arbitrary positive cover weights, the class of subsets of such mixed hosts is closed under finite unions and finite changes. For weighted supports use the union of the two finite prime sets: the prime part grows and h/(2h−1)h/(2^h-1) decreases. For two covers, interleave their finite sets with weights ηj/2\eta_j/2 and θj/2\theta_j/2; the total cost grows by at most two, since 2αj≤22^{\alpha_j}\le2. Subsets inherit the same hosts, and finite sets have finite weighted mass. This argument uses the positive-weight variant; it does not silently reindex the dyadic weights in [eq:257-strengthened-cover]. Countable unions require a tail budget. Every prime singleton is admitted, but for the full prime support 𝒫\mathcal P one has Δ2,𝒫(N)>1/3\Delta_{2,\mathcal P}(N)>1/3 for every N≥1N\ge1: indeed ∑r≥12−rω(N+r)≥1\sum_{r\ge1}2^{-r}\omega(N+r)\ge1, whereas X𝒫(2)≤∑a≥2(2a−1)−1<2/3X_{\mathcal P}(2)\le\sum_{a\ge2}(2^a-1)^{-1}<2/3. Here ω(n)\omega(n) is the number of distinct prime divisors of nn.

The elementary independence boundary.

For the divisor counts cAc_A and a fixed a∈Aa\in A, the identity cA(an)−cA(n)=1−𝟏a∣nc_A(an)-c_A(n)=1-\mathbf1_{a\mid n} holds for every n≥1n\ge1 exactly when aa is coprime to every other member of AA. Every summand 𝟏t∣an−𝟏t∣n\mathbf1_{t\mid an}-\mathbf1_{t\mid n} is nonnegative; t=at=a supplies the right side, and coprimality makes all other terms zero. If g=(a,t)>1g=(a,t)>1 for some t≠at\ne a, take n=t/gn=t/g to obtain an additional positive term. For distinct odd primes p,qp,q, the covariance of 𝟏2p∣n\mathbf1_{2p\mid n} and 𝟏2q∣n\mathbf1_{2q\mid n} over a common period is 1/(2pq)−1/(4pq)=1/(4pq)1/(2pq)-1/(4pq)=1/(4pq). Thus dilating a prime support already destroys the independence used in the prime-incidence argument. This brief ordinary calculation marks a boundary of that argument, not an irrationality criterion.

The universal problem and the half-value question

For an integer n≥1n \ge 1 set xn:=1/(2n−1)x_n := 1/(2^n-1), and for A⊆{1,2,3,…}A \subseteq \{1,2,3,\dots\} write xA:=∑n∈Axnx_A := \sum_{n \in A} x_n; the sum always converges, since xn=O(2−n)x_n = O(2^{-n}). Erdős’s Problem #257 asks a single universally quantified question about this family.

Definition 1.4 (Universal #257, written (U)). Is xA=∑n∈A1/(2n−1)x_A = \sum_{n \in A} 1/(2^n-1) irrational for every infinite A⊆ℕ>0A \subseteq \mathbb N_{>0}? OPEN. [Open]

Definition 1.5 (The half-value question, written (H)). Let the Mersenne achievement set be 𝒜:={y∈ℝ:∃A⊆ℕ,0∉A,y=∑n∈Axn}\mathcal{A} := \{\, y \in \mathbb{R} : \exists A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\ 0 \notin A,\ y = \sum_{n \in A} x_n \,\} (). Is 1/2∈𝒜1/2 \in \mathcal{A}? OPEN. [Open]

The two are joined by one elementary and completely one-sided implication. Every 2n−12^n-1 is odd, so every finite subset sum of {xn}\{x_n\} has odd reduced denominator and cannot equal 1/21/2 (). Hence a witness to 1/2∈𝒜1/2 \in \mathcal{A} is necessarily an infinite AA with xA=1/2x_A = 1/2 rational, which refutes (U) outright. Conversely, (U) implies 1/2∉𝒜1/2 \notin \mathcal{A} as one instance among uncountably many, and a proof of 1/2∉𝒜1/2 \notin \mathcal{A} leaves (U) entirely open. Thus (H) is one candidate counterexample to (U), not a restatement of it. Section 2.5 explains the corresponding difference between a finite certificate of nonmembership and an unbounded survival condition. [Math]

The reciprocal-summable and finite-prime weighted theorems, together with the checked support theorems below, leave (U) and (H) open. The later countermodels identify the particular arithmetic information lost by individual approaches; they do not prove that all such failures have one common cause.

Known support theorems

Full-support irrationality is Erdős’s theorem [1]. The pairwise-coprime case is Erdős’s theorem of 1968, where he also stated that the coprimality condition can be removed [2]. Luca and Tachiya proved irrationality for every purely periodic integer weight that is not identically zero [3]; the purely periodic, eventually periodic, residue-class, odd-support and periodic-weight rows below follow from their theorem, and odd support is their Example 2 . The lcm-gap supports, including factorials and powers of two, have summable reciprocals, so they fall under the reciprocal-summable theorem stated by Erdős. The Lean declarations in the table are formal proofs of these statements.

The following table includes two proof mechanisms: block certificates for the divisor counts cA(n)c_A(n), and rational-approximation estimates for a growing least-common-multiple gap. The latter need not be presented as instances of the former. The notation sc⁡A(n)\operatorname{sc}_A(n) in later source excerpts means the same function as cA(n)c_A(n). All bases in the table are integers b≥2b\ge2. For the lcm-gap row write Lk=lcm⁡(a0,…,ak−1)L_k=\operatorname{lcm}(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}), with L0=1L_0=1.

The lcm-gap hypothesis does imply reciprocal summability. Eventually ak+2>lcm⁡(ak,ak+1)a_{k+2}>\operatorname{lcm}(a_k,a_{k+1}). If ak+1≥2aka_{k+1}\ge2a_k, monotonicity gives ak+2>2aka_{k+2}>2a_k. Otherwise ak∤ak+1a_k\nmid a_{k+1}, so lcm⁡(ak,ak+1)≥2ak+1>2ak\operatorname{lcm}(a_k,a_{k+1})\ge2a_{k+1}>2a_k. Thus each of the even- and odd-indexed subsequences eventually grows geometrically, proving ∑k1/ak<∞\sum_k1/a_k<\infty. This explains the inclusion claimed above, rather than using “lacunary” as a substitute for a growth hypothesis. For eventually periodic weights, the periodic tail must not be identically zero: an eventually zero weight sequence gives only a finite rational sum.

Full-support irrationality for every integer base b≥2b\ge2 is classical (Erdős, 1948). The contribution recorded here is its Lean formalisation and the explicitly delimited structured-support developments, not a new extension from base two to arbitrary integer bases. Each support family retains its stated hypotheses; none establishes irrationality for every infinite support. The b=2b=2 case of the first row recovers the Erdős–Borwein constant E=∑n≥11/(2n−1)E = \sum_{n \ge 1} 1/(2^n-1) as a one-line corollary of that classical theorem. Separately, the independence and tail estimates used by a particular certificate construction must be checked for that support. Barrier 2.7 discusses those construction requirements; the averaging proof above does not assume pairwise coprimality or independence of divisor events.

A separate conditional result allows common factors confined to divisors of one fixed integer QQ, while the remaining factors must be pairwise coprime and have summable reciprocals (). It also assumes that for every K≥1K\ge1 there is an N≥0N\ge0 such that 2K∣∑r=1KcA(N+r)2K−r,∑r≥1cA(N+K+r)2−r≤16.2^K\mid\sum_{r=1}^K c_A(N+r)2^{K-r},\qquad \sum_{r\ge1}c_A(N+K+r)2^{-r}\le16. Thus relaxing coprimality does not remove the simultaneous divisibility and tail-bound requirement. This additional hypothesis is not proved here, and the source file does not establish a dichotomy for arbitrary supports. [Lean][Open]

The record also gives a logarithmic bound on runs of zero divisor counts under rationality: for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, a suitable constant BB bounds the length by εlog⁡2N+B\varepsilon\log_2N+B beyond the stated threshold (). For these supports there is already a simpler unconditional bound. If a0=min⁡Aa_0=\min A, every a0a_0 consecutive positive integers contain a multiple of a0a_0, where cAc_A is positive. Hence every zero run has length at most a0−1a_0-1, whether or not XA(2)X_A(2) is rational. In particular the logarithmic bound alone does not distinguish rational-valued supports. The separate unbounded-tail result also requires interpretation: an unbounded sequence can still satisfy u(N)=o(2N)u(N)=o(2^N). [Lean][Math]

Remark 1.6 (What is and is not covered in the universal direction). The pinned Lean corpus contains no theorem for A=A= the primes, but this is a formalisation boundary, not a mathematical open case: Tao and Teräväinen prove the base-22 prime-support value irrational by first identifying it with ∑n≥1ω(n)2−n\sum_{n\ge1}\omega(n)2^{-n}. Duverney and Tachiya likewise settle squarefree support at every power-of-two base, and the perfect iith powers at every integer base (Corollary 1.2 and Example 1.1, p. 4 of the author preprint). Neither result is formalised here. The statement of Problem #257 has been formalised before, as a conjecture with an unfilled proof, in the Formal Conjectures collection; that file also proves the Lambert identity for the full-support value and states its irrationality, the 1948 theorem of Erdős, with proof sorry. It is statement-level prior art, and no theorem recorded here is derived from it. The corpus still has no general theorem for an arbitrary positive-density nonperiodic or divisor-dense support, and the universal statement remains open.

Periodic weights: the two hypothesis sets.

The periodic sequence theorem belongs to Luca and Tachiya ; their later author-written account states it as Theorem A . In the displayed Lean row above, nonnegativity and frequent nonvanishing are assumptions on cw(n)=∑d∣nw(d)c_w(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}w(d), not on w(n)w(n) itself. The formal row must therefore be read as a separately specified instance, not as an exact transcription of every clause of the published theorem.

A separate denominator-growth criterion.

Erdős’s growth theorem [21], as restated and recovered by Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kovač and Zhang [22], gives irrationality of ∑n1/an\sum_n1/a_n for an increasing integer sequence with an≥n1+τa_n\ge n^{1+\tau} for some τ>0\tau>0 and limsup⁡nan1/2n=∞\limsup_n a_n^{1/2^n}=\infty. For an=bcn−1a_n=b^{c_n}-1, where cnc_n are increasing positive exponents and b≥2b\ge2 is an integer, the growth hypothesis becomes limsupn→∞cn2n=∞.\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{c_n}{2^n}=\infty. Indeed cn≥nc_n\ge n, so the polynomial lower bound holds eventually, and log⁡b(bcn−1)=cn+O(1)\log_b(b^{c_n}-1)=c_n+O(1). An eventual lower bound suffices: deleting finitely many terms subtracts a rational number and changes 2n2^n only by a fixed factor after reindexing.

This is not the reciprocal-summability condition of the reciprocal-support theorem in Section 1.1. The squares cn=n2c_n=n^2 have convergent reciprocal sum but cn/2n→0c_n/2^n\to0. In the other direction, set n1=1n_1=1 and nk+1=nk+4nkn_{k+1}=n_k+4^{n_k}, and let block kk consist of all integers from 4nk4^{n_k} to 2⋅4nk−12\cdot4^{n_k}-1. The blocks are successive disjoint increasing blocks, and their union has increasing enumeration satisfying cnk=4nkc_{n_k}=4^{n_k}. Thus cnk/2nk=2nk→∞c_{n_k}/2^{n_k}=2^{n_k}\to\infty, whereas each block has reciprocal sum at least 1/21/2. Its reciprocal sum therefore diverges. These examples separate these two hypotheses, not every support criterion in this paper. [Cited][Math]

Geometry and rational-target membership

Theorem 1.7 (Achievement-set geometry). 𝒜\mathcal{A} is compact, closed, perfect, totally disconnected and nowhere dense, and volume⁡(𝒜)=1\operatorname{volume}(\mathcal{A}) = 1. Thus its measure is positive although it contains no interval. Its convex hull is [0,E][0,E], where E=∑n≥1wnE=\sum_{n\ge1}w_n. The positive-index digit coding onto 𝒜\mathcal{A} is injective: each achievable real has exactly one support. achievement-set (uniform) [Lean]

Theorem 1.8 (Support-restricted refinement). Use zero-based indices in this statement: coordinate j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} carries weight wj+1w_{j+1}. For J⊆ℕJ\subseteq\mathbb{N}, consider the sums that use only coordinates in JJ. If ℕ∖J\mathbb{N}\smallsetminus J is finite, this achievement set has measure 2−|ℕ∖J|2^{-|\mathbb{N}\smallsetminus J|}; if infinitely many coordinates are omitted, its measure is zero. Injectivity survives every restriction; perfectness is proved when JJ is infinite. No perfectness claim is made for finite JJ, whose coding range is finite. achievement-set (uniform) [Lean]

Hausdorff dimension of a restricted set.

For example, retaining the positive exponents 2,4,6,…2,4,6,\ldots gives a set of measure zero but Hausdorff dimension 1/21/2. More generally, let J⊆{1,2,…}J\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots\} and put SJ={∑n∈Jεnwn:εn∈{0,1}},sN=#(J∩{1,…,N}),d=liminfN→∞sN/N.S_J=\left\{\sum_{n\in J}\varepsilon_nw_n: \varepsilon_n\in\{0,1\}\right\},\qquad s_N=\#(J\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}),\qquad d=\liminf_{N\to\infty}s_N/N. Then dim⁡HSJ=d\dim_H S_J=d. Here is a proof, separate from the supplied formal measure statements. If JJ is finite, both sides are zero, so suppose JJ is infinite.

Write wn=2−n+δnw_n=2^{-n}+\delta_n, where δn=∑r≥22−rn\delta_n=\sum_{r\ge2}2^{-rn}. A geometric sum gives ∑k>nδk=∑r≥22−rn2r−1≤δn/3<δn.\sum_{k>n}\delta_k =\sum_{r\ge2}\frac{2^{-rn}}{2^r-1}\le\delta_n/3<\delta_n. The unique Mersenne digit coding therefore defines a map from SJS_J onto the binary digit-restricted set BJ={∑n∈Jεn2−n}B_J=\{\sum_{n\in J}\varepsilon_n2^{-n}\} by keeping the same digits. This map is 11-Lipschitz. In fact, at the first differing digit nn, the binary difference is nonnegative after orienting the larger digit first, and the Mersenne difference exceeds it by at least δn−∑k>nδk>0\delta_n-\sum_{k>n}\delta_k>0.

The 2sN2^{s_N} Mersenne prefix intervals have length at most RN≤21−NR_N\le2^{1-N}. For any t>dt>d, a subsequence with sN/N<(d+t)/2s_N/N<(d+t)/2 makes their total tt-power length tend to zero. Hence dim⁡HSJ≤d\dim_H S_J\le d. For the reverse inequality, give the allowed binary digits independent probabilities 1/21/2. Each dyadic interval of length 2−N2^{-N} has measure at most 2−sN2^{-s_N}; endpoints have measure zero because JJ is infinite. An interval II with 2−N−1<|I|≤2−N2^{-N-1}<|I|\le2^{-N} meets at most three such dyadic intervals. For 0<s<d0<s<d and all sufficiently large NN, its measure is therefore at most 3⋅2−sN≤3⋅2s|I|s3\cdot2^{-s_N}\le3\cdot2^s|I|^s. Summing this inequality over any sufficiently fine cover of BJB_J gives a positive lower bound for the sum of its ss-power lengths. Thus dim⁡HBJ≥s\dim_H B_J\ge s; letting s↑ds\uparrow d proves dim⁡HBJ≥d\dim_H B_J\ge d. A Lipschitz map cannot increase Hausdorff dimension, since it sends a cover to one of no larger diameters. The map above now yields dim⁡HSJ≥d\dim_H S_J\ge d, as required. For d=0d=0 the lower bound is automatic. [Math]

Remark 1.9 (Achievement-set terminology and source boundary). We use the modern term achievement set for the subsum set that Kakeya’s 1914 note describes as a set of partial sums. For an infinite summable sequence of positive terms, Kakeya proves perfectness, and nowhere density under an all-index strict-tail condition; Kovač–Tao, Remark 4.1 verifies that strict-tail condition for the fixed-base Mersenne weights. Nitecki proves that a subsum set whose terms all exceed their tails is a Cantor set of measure lim⁡n2nRn\lim_n2^nR_n, and credits this to Hornich [4]; this is the classical source for the topology and measure used here. The local volume dichotomy, injectivity, and greedy-membership statements above and below are Lean-checked claims of this corpus. The sparse power-series criteria of Kaneko–Suzuki–Tachiya (Theorems 1–3, pp. 3–5 of arXiv v1) assume sparse coefficient supports; their relation to the divisor-incidence coefficients of these subseries is recorded after Theorem 1.1. Remark 1.11 (Literature, exactly). EE is irrational [1]. Zudilin proves the irrationality measure bound μ(E)≤2.46497868…\mu(E)\le2.46497868\ldots , correcting an earlier computation (see the remark at the end of his Section 3, p. 159). Transcendence of EE is unknown [6], and the Erdős–Graham conjecture that every such subset sum is irrational, i.e. (U), is itself open. For the binary digits of EE, Erdős’s proof produces arbitrarily long runs of zeros. Crandall asked whether the block 11 occurs infinitely often in the binary expansion of EE, and Campbell proves that it does [9]. [Cited]

The cited digit results establish the occurrence of particular patterns. An irrationality-measure estimate gives a different kind of information: a run of LL equal digits after position NN approximates EE by a dyadic rational with denominator at most 2N2^N, giving L<(μ(E)−1+ε)NL<(\mu(E)-1+\varepsilon)N for all sufficiently large NN. The reset argument considered here needs a bound for runs in its own inhomogeneous recurrence, not simply in the binary digits of EE. No implication from the cited digit results to that bound is proved here. Such a bound is an input to this particular approach to (H), not a necessary ingredient of every possible proof of membership.

II. Limitations and extensions of recorded methods

Limitations of the recorded methods

What the obstructions do and do not show

This section studies the scope of particular reformulations and certificate mechanisms. Several share the greedy representation, but no proof identifies a single necessary obstruction to all methods. The statements below are useful insofar as they specify which hypotheses fail, which implications are equivalences, and which parameters must be uniform. The first structural fact is uniqueness at a fixed target and depth.

Observation 2.1 (Uniqueness within the fixed-target coding). Each Mersenne weight exceeds the sum of all subsequent weights. Consequently the digit coding is injective (Theorem 1.7): a represented target has only one support, recovered by the greedy rule. For the integer weights, both the scale and the cutoff matter. If 2≤k≤M2\le k\le M and qM,d=⌊2M/(2d−1)⌋q_{M,d}=\lfloor2^M/(2^d-1)\rfloor for 2≤d≤k2\le d\le k, then qM,d−∑e=d+1kqM,e≥2M−k.q_{M,d}-\sum_{e=d+1}^{k}q_{M,e}\ge2^{M-k}. Indeed, with wd=(2d−1)−1w_d=(2^d-1)^{-1} and Rk=∑e>kweR_k=\sum_{e>k}w_e, wd−∑e=d+1kwe=wd−Rd+Rk>Rk>2−k.w_d-\sum_{e=d+1}^{k}w_e=w_d-R_d+R_k>R_k>2^{-k}. Rounding the head down loses less than one, while rounding the later terms down can only increase the difference. The resulting integer is greater than 2M−k−12^{M-k}-1, proving the bound. Comparing two words at their first differing rank gives the same separation for their sums. The rows with M=2sM=2s, k=s−1k=s-1 and s≥3s\ge3 therefore have gap at least 2s+12^{s+1}; the full rows with k=Mk=M have gap at least 11. The first bound must not be applied after enlarging the cutoff: at M=6M=6, adjoining rank 33 introduces the subset sum q6,3=9<16=23+1q_{6,3}=9<16=2^{3+1}.

When a finite construction is proved to encode a fixed greedy target, its choices are constrained by that support. Injectivity alone does not identify an arbitrary finite approximation with a real greedy prefix. Nor does it exclude averaging over indices, moduli, nearby targets or auxiliary constructions. meta (uniform) [Lean][Math]
Sources: , , .

The six limitations below require separate arguments. Fixed-target uniqueness explains canonicalisation (2.2); the recorded identities determine which sufficient conditions are equivalent to their goal (2.3). Measure and category (2.6), observation scales (2.4), finite versus infinite membership (2.5), and the hypotheses of the support certificate (2.7) do not follow from injectivity alone.

Proof. For (i), truncate DD at each successive rank. The target remains in the corresponding prefix interval because all discarded terms are bounded by the complete tail. The two child intervals are disjoint: the lower one forces a greedy skip and the upper one forces a greedy take. Induction identifies every digit. Part (ii) implies (i) at depth c−1c-1, since wc<Rc−1w_c<R_{c-1}. For (iii), consider the first disagreement with the integer greedy word. Taking a rejected weight would exceed TT; rejecting an accepted weight leaves a deficit at least gg, even after taking every later weight. The converse is immediate. ◻

Excludes at fixed depth. Under the three canonicalisation hypotheses just stated, a proof cannot gain freedom by choosing a different admissible word for the same target and depth. This says nothing about families satisfying different approximation conditions, or about averaging over depths or auxiliary data.

Equivalent formulations of half-membership

The six conditions listed below are equivalent to half-membership. Their quantifier patterns can look less restrictive than a single compatible infinite construction, but the equivalences must be checked mathematically. They follow here from a carry identity and an unconditional tail estimate. No claim is made that every conceivable sufficient condition is equivalent to the goal.

The known prime-support theorem

The base-22 prime-support value is not an open target: ∑pprime12p−1=∑n≥1ω(n)2n\sum_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}\frac1{2^p-1} =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\omega(n)}{2^n} by expanding each reciprocal Mersenne term geometrically and collecting divisors. Tao and Teräväinen prove the right-hand series irrational in Theorem 1.3 of Quantitative correlations and some problems on prime factors of consecutive integers. Their proof is analytic and is cited here; it is not formalised in the pinned Lean corpus.

The local pairwise-coprime certificate theorem still does not cover the primes because it assumes summability of ∑p1/p\sum_p1/p. That is a boundary of this engine, not a boundary of the mathematics. The previously proposed windowed-tail repair is therefore withdrawn as a research contribution. It may remain useful as an audit question about whether the existing Lean engine can reproduce the known theorem, but reproducing a cited result is not new progress on #257. After Theorem 1.3 the authors state the prime-support extension to every integer base b≥2b\ge2 and, separately, the full prime-power result at base 22, leaving those modifications to the reader. These statements should not be combined into an attributed all-base theorem for arbitrary prime-power subsets.

Proposition 2.7 lists the equivalent conditions: a pointwise upper bound on CGC_G, infinitely many skipped ranks, exact quotient sums at unbounded depths, and the two cofinal carry bounds. For the carry conditions, the residual identity and its tail estimates are the relevant inputs: , , , and, for the terminal-strip conditions, evaluation of the square root at a perfect square. The one-sided scope limitation in Proposition 2.7 still applies to general supports.

Purpose of the equivalences. These results identify the exact logical content of the proposed hypotheses. They do not settle half-membership, nor do they make an equivalent formulation useless: a different expression of the same condition may expose an invariant or a more convenient induction. The formalisation task is separate from the unproved arithmetic assertion on either side.

Route 3 must be compared with the external prime-support theorem of Tao and Teräväinen ; reproducing it in this framework requires its own analytic input. Route 2 offers a different finite search space under the conditions stated there. Routes 1 and 5 share some incidence identities, but this is not a proof that every missing hypothesis is equivalent. The appropriate comparison is the input each route needs, its quantifiers, and what a successful estimate would imply.

Reading the detailed record

The opening note has already defined the evidence bands, scale tags, coordinates, and catalogue terminology. The longer record has two different reading modes, and they should not be confused.

Read linearly.

Sections 2 and 3 form one argument: the first identifies the recurring obstructions, and the second isolates the routes those obstructions do not exclude. Read them in order before selecting a new attack.

Use as reference.

The mathematical-ingredient catalogue may be entered by coordinate: the certificate method and universal-direction record; the greedy and achievement-set geometry; the integer-quotient model, quotient identity, and dynamics; the half-carry and Boolean–Möbius coordinates; and the support rigidity results. The later implication tables record what chains with what, while the near-miss index gives the exact mismatch at each open obligation.

Scale and coordinate discipline.

The direct certified instances remain fixed or bounded; rungs J≤22J \le 22, seam rows ≤200,000\le 200{,}000, ranks ≤3000\le 3000, and macro depth ≤13,548,057\le 13{,}548{,}057; whereas the open obligations are cofinal. Theorem 2.11 shows that extending a bounded range does not establish a cofinal statement. Coordinate tags are equally literal: an obstruction in half-carry recurrence, quotient-row, or diophantine does not transfer to another representation without a proved map. Coordinate-free barriers are marked explicitly.

III. Detailed statement and arithmetic catalogue

The series, the greedy rule and finite identities

The object

In this part, write xn=wn=(2n−1)−1x_n=w_n=(2^n-1)^{-1} for every positive integer nn, and xA=XA(2)=∑n∈Axnx_A=X_A(2)=\sum_{n\in A}x_n for A⊆ℕ>0A\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}. These series converge by comparison with ∑n2−n\sum_n2^{-n}. Exponent 11 contributes the rational number x1=1x_1=1, so deleting or adjoining it does not affect irrationality. It cannot occur in a representation of 1/21/2; those calculations therefore start at exponent 22.

Definition 5.1 (Universal Problem #257). Is xA=∑n∈A1/(2n−1)x_A = \sum_{n \in A} 1/(2^n-1) irrational for every infinite A⊆ℕ>0A \subseteq \mathbb{N}_{>0}? The quantifier ranges over all infinite sets of positive exponents. It is OPEN. [Open]

The support theorems prove irrationality for specified infinite families. The following question instead asks whether one particular rational number is represented. A positive answer would disprove the universal assertion; a negative answer would settle only that target. The later analysis also treats 1/211/21.

Definition 5.2 (The distinguished half-value question). Define the Mersenne achievement set 𝒜:={y∈ℝ:∃A⊆ℕ,0∉A,y=∑n∈Axn}\mathcal{A} := \{\,y \in \mathbb{R} : \exists A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\ 0 \notin A,\ y = \sum_{n \in A} x_n\,\}, the set of reals realizable as a subset sum of the positive-index Mersenne weights {xn}n≥1\{x_n\}_{n \ge 1}. Is 1/2∈𝒜1/2 \in \mathcal{A}? This is OPEN. [Open]

Observation 5.3 (Why the half-value question controls universal #257). Any finite subset sum of {xn}\{x_n\} has odd reduced denominator, since every 2n−12^n - 1 is odd; hence no finite AA can sum to 1/21/2 (). Consequently, if 1/2∈𝒜1/2 \in \mathcal{A}, the witnessing support AA is necessarily infinite, and xA=1/2x_A = 1/2 is rational. Such an AA is then a single infinite set for which the universal-#257 sum is rational – an outright refutation of universal #257. Conversely, universal #257 being true forces 1/2∉𝒜1/2 \notin \mathcal{A} as one instance among uncountably many. The half-value question is therefore one concrete test of the negation, not a restatement of the universal problem. Excluding 1/21/2 would not exclude every other rational value, even though the support theorems already settle many infinite families. Representing 1/21/2 would give an infinite-support counterexample to the universal assertion. (n/a) [Math]

What is proved
Full-support irrationality, for every base

Theorem 5.4 (Full-support irrationality, unconditional, every base b≥2b \ge 2). For every integer b≥2b \ge 2, ∑k=0∞1bk+1−1is irrational.\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{b^{k+1}-1} \quad \text{is irrational.} Hypotheses: b∈ℕb \in \mathbb{N}, b≥2b \ge 2. Conclusion: unconditional irrationality of the full-support Erdős–Borwein-type series at every base, not merely base 22. full-support (uniform) [Lean]
Source: (‘b:ℕb : \mathbb{N}, hb : 2≤b2 \le b’), recorded via a certificate machine (bounded Bertrand/CRT first-block frame, middle-window divisor-pair average with pigeonhole selection, explicit parameter closure). The base-22 instance recovering the classical Erdős–Borwein constant’s irrationality is , a one-line corollary.

This formalizes the positive-integer-base scope of Erdős’s classical 1948 full-support theorem, which already covered integer bases of absolute value greater than one. The base-two Erdős–Borwein constant is a particular case; the Lean theorem is recorded with no open hypotheses.

Structured infinite supports

Beyond full support (A={1,2,3,…}A = \{1,2,3,\dots\}, i.e. m=1m=1 below), the following named infinite families are proved irrational for every integer base b≥2b\ge2. The purely periodic, eventually periodic, residue-class and odd supports follow from the periodic theorem of Luca and Tachiya , and the declarations below are formal proofs of these cases:

Theorem 5.5 (Purely periodic support). For integers b≥2b\ge2 and m≥1m\ge1, and every mm-periodic A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb N (i.e. n+m∈A⇔n∈An+m \in A \Leftrightarrow n \in A for all nn) containing a positive element, the support series ∑a∈A,a≥1(ba−1)−1\sum_{a\in A,\ a\ge1}(b^a-1)^{-1} is irrational. Hypotheses: b≥2b \ge 2, m≥1m \ge 1, AA mm-periodic, ∃a>0,a∈A\exists a > 0,\ a \in A. periodic-support (uniform) [Lean]
Source: .

Theorem 5.6 (Eventually periodic support). For integers b≥2b\ge2 and m≥1m\ge1, if A⊆ℕA\subseteq\mathbb N is infinite and its membership is mm-periodic from some threshold N0N_0 on (i.e. n+m∈A⇔n∈An+m \in A \Leftrightarrow n \in A for all n≥N0n \ge N_0), then ∑a∈A,a≥1(ba−1)−1\sum_{a\in A,\ a\ge1}(b^a-1)^{-1} is irrational, by transferring irrationality across the finite symmetric difference from the shifted purely periodic set Apure:={n:n+mN0∈A}A_{\mathrm{pure}} := \{n : n + m N_0 \in A\}. Hypotheses: b≥2b \ge 2, m≥1m \ge 1, N0∈ℕN_0 \in \mathbb{N}, eventual mm-periodicity from N0N_0, AA infinite. eventually-periodic-support (uniform) [Lean]
Source: .

Theorem 5.7 (Residue-class support). For integers b≥2b\ge2, m≥1m\ge1 and cc, the series ∑n≥1,n≡c(mod⁡m)(bn−1)−1\sum_{n\ge1,\ n\equiv c\pmod m}(b^n-1)^{-1} is irrational. residue-class-support (uniform) [Lean]
Source: (specializes purely periodic support).

Lean: irrational_residueClass_positive_support.

Theorem 5.8 (Odd support). For every integer b≥2b\ge2, the series ∑n≥1,n odd(bn−1)−1\sum_{n\ge1,\ n\text{ odd}}(b^n-1)^{-1} is irrational. This density-1/21/2 support is the case treated explicitly by Luca and Tachiya . odd-support (uniform) [Lean]
Source: (specializes residue-class support at m=2,c=1m=2,c=1).

A support representing 1/21/2 cannot be eventually periodic, by these irrationality theorems. This is a restriction on a hypothetical representation, not a proof that the actual greedy support is nonperiodic: if the greedy construction fails, it eventually selects every exponent. The periodic-support results therefore decide neither alternative for 1/2∈𝒜1/2\in\mathcal A.

Topology and measure of the achievement set

Theorem 5.9 (Achievement-set topology and measure). 𝒜\mathcal{A} (Definition 5.2) is compact, closed, perfect, totally disconnected, and nowhere dense; its Lebesgue measure is exactly 11: volume⁡(𝒜)=1\operatorname{volume}(\mathcal{A}) = 1. Hypotheses: none. Conclusion: 𝒜\mathcal A is a Cantor set of positive measure, often called a fat Cantor set. Its measure is 11, not the length of its ambient interval [0,E][0,E], where E≈1.6067E\approx1.6067. achievement-set-topology (n/a) [Lean]
Source: , , , , , . Strict separation and summability give the compactness, unique coding, and Cantor topology, and Hornich’s strict-tail theorem, as proved by Nitecki [4], gives the measure as lim⁡N2NRN\lim_N2^NR_N with RN=∑n>NxnR_N=\sum_{n>N}x_n: each level-NN cylinder has length RNR_N, and the 2N2^N disjoint cylinders have total length 2NRN2^NR_N. The Mersenne-specific input is 2NRN→12^NR_N\to1. Other weight sequences require their own tail asymptotic.
Use: Theorem 5.10 below (compactness is exactly what powers every “limit of achieved points is achieved” argument used downstream, including the seam-limit route of Part 2).

Lean: paper_achievement_geometry, mersenne_topology_quantitative.

Theorem 5.10 (Membership equals greedy survival at every level). For a real xx, let rn(x)r_n(x) be its greedy remainder after rank nn, and let Rn=∑j>nwjR_n=\sum_{j>n}w_j, as in the initial notation. Then x∈𝒜⇔x≥0andrn(x)≤Rn for every n≥0.x\in\mathcal A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\ge0\ \text{and}\ r_n(x)\le R_n\text{ for every }n\ge0. The inequality says that the unselected tail has enough total mass at every rank. A failure at any one rank excludes membership; the inequalities at all ranks give a representation. greedy-survival (uniform) [Lean]
Source: (forward direction , reverse ).

The greedy rule for one half

Fix the target 1/21/2 and the weights xn=1/(2n−1)x_n = 1/(2^n-1). Here x1=1x_1=1, so exponent one cannot occur in a representation of 1/21/2 by positive summands; the half-target discussion starts at exponent two. (The reciprocal formula is undefined only at exponent zero.) The greedy rule is deterministic. Strict tail domination makes it recover the support of any represented target (Theorem 5.10):

Definition 5.11 (The half-value greedy orbit). Let ρk=rk−1(1/2)\rho_k=r_{k-1}(1/2) be the residual entering rank kk, so ρ2=1/2\rho_2=1/2. In this subsection xk=wkx_k=w_k and Tk+1=Rk=∑j>kwjT_{k+1}=R_k=\sum_{j>k}w_j. At rank k≥2k\ge2:

  • Take iff ρk≥xk\rho_k \ge x_k; if taken, ρk+1:=ρk−xk\rho_{k+1} := \rho_k - x_k.

  • Skip otherwise; ρk+1:=ρk\rho_{k+1} := \rho_k.

A skip at rank kk is:

  • safe iff ρk≤Tk+1:=∑j>kxj\rho_k \le T_{k+1} := \sum_{j>k} x_j (the total remaining mass does not yet rule out a representation; this inequality alone does not guarantee one);

  • fatal iff ρk∈(Tk+1,xk)\rho_k \in (T_{k+1}, x_k) (the residual is too large for the remaining tail to ever reach, yet too small to have been taken at kk – an impossible gap).

For example, ranks 22 and 33 are selected, leaving 1/2−1/3−1/7=1/421/2-1/3-1/7=1/42. Ranks 44 and 55 are skipped, while rank 66 is selected and leaves 1/1261/126. These decisions illustrate the rule; they do not establish its infinite survival.

By Theorem 5.10, 1/2∈𝒜1/2 \in \mathcal{A} iff no rank of this orbit is ever fatal. Two boundary degeneracies are excluded unconditionally and independently of any open hypothesis:

Remark 5.12 (No-ties: both greedy-orbit boundaries are strict). (a) ρk≠xk\rho_k \ne x_k at any rank: a finite Mersenne sum has odd reduced denominator (each 2n−12^n-1 is odd), so the residual 1/21/2 minus a finite prefix cannot equal the odd-denominator number xkx_k, sharpening the general denominator-parity fact used in Observation 5.3. (b) ρk≠Tk+1\rho_k \ne T_{k+1} at any rank: the tail Tk+1=E−1−∑2≤j≤kxjT_{k+1} = E - 1 - \sum_{2 \le j \le k} x_j, where E:=∑n≥1xnE := \sum_{n\ge1} x_n is the Erdős–Borwein constant, is irrational by Erdős’s own 1948 theorem (the base-22 case of Theorem 5.4), while ρk\rho_k is always rational; equality is impossible. Conclusion: both greedy-orbit boundaries are provably strict at every rank, so the orbit’s decisions stabilize after finitely many strict inequalities at any fixed truncation depth. no-ties (uniform) [Math]

Integer quotients and their remainder identity

The quotient rows are finite integer approximations to the real greedy rule, not identical finite stages of that rule. Their normalised weights tend to the Mersenne weights and their targets tend to 1/21/2. Proposition 8.1 proves agreement at each fixed prefix once the row index is sufficiently large; it does not assert simultaneous agreement at all ranks. Fix a row n≥6n\ge6. The integer quotient weights at row nn are w(n,d):=⌊4n2d−1⌋,d=2,…,n−1,w(n,d) := \left\lfloor \frac{4^n}{2^d-1} \right\rfloor, \qquad d = 2,\dots,n-1, and the integer target is Tn:=22n−1−2nT_n := 2^{2n-1} - 2^n. The integer greedy process takes ranks d=2,…,n−1d = 2,\dots,n-1 in ascending order against TnT_n exactly as in Definition 5.11, producing a take set Dn⊆{2,…,n−1}D_n \subseteq \{2,\dots,n-1\} and skip set Skipn:={2,…,n−1}∖Dn\mathrm{Skip}_n := \{2,\dots,n-1\} \mathbin{\backslash} D_n. Define the integer remainder rem(n):=Tn−∑d∈Dnw(n,d)\mathrm{rem}(n) := T_n - \sum_{d \in D_n} w(n,d) and the scaled remainder deviation Δn:=rem(n)−2n\Delta_n := \mathrm{rem}(n) - 2^n.

Definition 5.13 (The full-support quotient recurrence). For M≥2M \ge 2, define K(M):=2M−1−∑d=2M⌊2M2d−1⌋.K(M) := 2^{M-1} - \sum_{d=2}^{M} \left\lfloor \frac{2^M}{2^d-1} \right\rfloor. This depends only on MM, not on the selected support in a quotient row. The floor-quotient recurrence gives K(2)=1,K(M+1)=2K(M)−(τ(M+1)−1).K(2)=1,\qquad K(M+1)=2K(M)-(\tau(M+1)-1). Here τ(n)\tau(n) counts the positive divisors of nn. To see the correction term, double the quotients for 2≤d≤M2\le d\le M and add one for each such dd dividing M+1M+1. The new endpoint d=M+1d=M+1 contributes one more quotient. Together these are exactly the τ(M+1)−1\tau(M+1)-1 divisors at least two. This is an identity for every M≥2M\ge2, not merely a checked finite recurrence. universal-recursion (uniform) [Math][Cert]

Theorem 5.14 (Decomposition of the integer remainder). For every quotient row n≥6n \ge 6, Δn=K(2n)+∑d∈Skipn⌊4n2d−1⌋.\begin{equation*} \Delta_n \;=\; K(2n) \;+\; \sum_{d \in \mathrm{Skip}_n} \left\lfloor \frac{4^n}{2^d-1} \right\rfloor. \tag{I} \end{equation*} Here the take and skip sets, capacity and remainder are those defined at the start of this subsection. The identity separates the contribution of the full exponent range from that of the omitted ranks. It makes no claim that there are few omitted ranks; controlling their sum is a separate part of any application. quotient-row ; integer-greedy (Mersenne weights, binary digits of KK) (fixed) [Math][Cert]
Proof. For d=nd=n the quotient is 2n+12^n+1, and for n<d≤2nn<d\le2n it is 22n−d2^{2n-d}. Hence ∑d=n2n⌊4n2d−1⌋=2n+1+∑j=0n−12j=2n+1.\sum_{d=n}^{2n}\left\lfloor\frac{4^n}{2^d-1}\right\rfloor =2^n+1+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}2^j=2^{n+1}. Substitute this in the definition of K(2n)K(2n), split {2,…,n−1}=Dn⊔Skipn\{2,\ldots,n-1\}=D_n\sqcup\mathrm{Skip}_n, and use Δn=22n−1−2n+1−∑d∈Dnw(n,d)\Delta_n=2^{2n-1}-2^{n+1}-\sum_{d\in D_n}w(n,d). This gives (I). Certification: verified rows 6≤n≤2006\le n\le200, zero mismatches, reported as reproduced in two separate computations (§5.7).
Use: (I) permits substitution of information about K(2n)K(2n). A resulting estimate for Δn\Delta_n must also retain or bound the skip-set sum; information about KK alone need not control their cancellation.

A real-valued form of the quotient identity

Theorem 5.15 (Real (non-integer) form of the quotient identity). Let xd:=1/(2d−1)x_d := 1/(2^d-1) and define the constant C:=∑d≥2xd−12=E−32=0.1066951524152917…,C \;:=\; \sum_{d \ge 2} x_d \;-\; \tfrac12 \;=\; E - \tfrac32 \;=\; 0.1066951524152917\ldots, where EE is the Erdős–Borwein constant. Then, for every quotient row n≥6n \ge 6, Δn=4n(∑d∈Skipnxd−C)+ηn,|ηn|<2n+2.\begin{equation*} \Delta_n \;=\; 4^n \Big( \sum_{d \in \mathrm{Skip}_n} x_d \;-\; C \Big) \;+\; \eta_n, \qquad |\eta_n| < 2n+2. \tag{II} \end{equation*} Proof. Splitting the full series at nn gives ηn=4nRn−1−2n+1+∑d∈Dn{4n2d−1}.\eta_n=4^nR_{n-1}-2^{n+1} +\sum_{d\in D_n}\left\{\frac{4^n}{2^d-1}\right\}. The tail bounds 2−(n−1)<Rn−1≤2−(n−1)+234−(n−1)2^{-(n-1)}<R_{n-1}\le 2^{-(n-1)}+\tfrac23 4^{-(n-1)} and |Dn|≤n−2|D_n|\le n-2 show 0<ηn<n+2/3<2n+20<\eta_n<n+2/3<2n+2.

Use of the error bound. For H>2n+2H>2n+2, the condition |∑d∈Skipnxd−C|>(H+2n+2)/4n|\sum_{d\in\mathrm{Skip}_n}x_d-C|>(H+2n+2)/4^n is sufficient for |Δn|>H|\Delta_n|>H. Conversely, |Δn|>H|\Delta_n|>H implies |∑d∈Skipnxd−C|>(H−2n−2)/4n|\sum_{d\in\mathrm{Skip}_n}x_d-C|>(H-2n-2)/4^n. Thus a square-root-exponential deviation corresponds to a separation of order 2−3n/22^{-3n/2}, with the displayed additive error retained. This is not an exact equivalence after simply discarding that error. real approximation and integer remainder (uniform) [Math]

Dynamics

Theorem 5.16 (Exact recurrences for the three branches). Fix n≥5n\ge5. Among the quotient sums over subsets of {2,…,n−1}\{2,\ldots,n-1\}, let DnD_n give the largest sum at most TnT_n and let BnB_n give the smallest sum strictly greater than TnT_n. Thus DnD_n is the greedy support already defined. Put r=rem(n),o=Q(Bn,2n)−Tn,r=\mathrm{rem}(n),\qquad o=Q(B_n,2n)-T_n, and define the two correction terms by p−=∑d∈Dn(2𝟏d∣2n+1+𝟏d∣2n+2),p+=∑d∈Bn(2𝟏d∣2n+1+𝟏d∣2n+2).p^- =\sum_{d\in D_n}\bigl(2\mathbf1_{d\mid2n+1} +\mathbf1_{d\mid2n+2}\bigr),\qquad p^+ =\sum_{d\in B_n}\bigl(2\mathbf1_{d\mid2n+1} +\mathbf1_{d\mid2n+2}\bigr). The old quotient sums are separated by at least gg, so the corrected sums remain separated by at least 4g−2(n−2)>2g+44g-2(n-2)>2g+4. This exceeds the new terminal weight. The upper word exists: already the terms at d=2,3,4d=2,3,4 have sum greater than TnT_n for n≥5n\ge5, since 1/3+1/7+1/15=19/35>1/21/3+1/7+1/15=19/35>1/2 and their total floor error is less than 33. Moreover, the increment Tn+1−4Tn=gT_{n+1}-4T_n=g is smaller than this separation, so no old word beyond the adjacent upper one can fit. It is therefore enough to compare the two adjacent old words and the terminal weight. The upper word fits precisely under the condition U\mathrm U; its remainder is then too small to take the terminal weight. Otherwise the lower word is used, and comparison with the terminal weight gives M\mathrm M or R\mathrm R. Substitution yields the displayed formulas. Use: truncated weights define a different greedy problem, and the quotient-row construction uses integer weights rather than the original real weights. These are not automatically four readings of the same decision stream. Their relevance to full-weight membership comes from the approximation, limit, or identification theorems cited for each construction. A certificate at one range does not transfer to another without such a theorem, and these reports do not decide the universal problem.

The large computation ranges in this section are inherited from their identified sources. The source tags retain the distinction between formal proofs and reported finite checks; neither should be read as a new replay of those computations.

Detailed results and their hypotheses

This section catalogues machinery for Erdős #257 (is ∑n∈A1/(2n−1)\sum_{n\in A} 1/(2^n-1) irrational for every infinite A⊆ℕ≥1A\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}?) drawn from the half-membership route (is 1/21/2 in the Mersenne achievement set?) and the support-rigidity / full-support route (irrationality of ∑a∈A1/(2a−1)\sum_{a\in A} 1/(2^a-1) for named families AA). Every entry states exact hypotheses, exact conclusion, coordinate, scale, evidence band, and Lean source location. None of these results decides #257. Entries are grouped into conditional implications (with any unproved hypothesis identified) and equivalences and exact identities (including structural properties, definitions and exact finite values). The scale labels distinguish a single instance, a bounded range, unbounded depths and a uniform assertion. They are descriptions of quantifiers, not a total ordering of the strength of the results.

Theorem 6.31 (The half-skip dichotomy via Erdős–Borwein irrationality). Consequence theorems

This subsection concerns finite sets DD whose floor-quotient sums nearly represent 1/21/2. Its main implication is elementary to state: if such finite sums approximate 1/21/2 at unbounded depths with an error tending to zero, compactness supplies a representing support. The difficult input is the existence of the finite sets, not the final compactness argument. Definitions and conditional implications are separated below. A hypothesis marked [Open] is not established merely because the implication using it has a formal proof.

Uniqueness for gap-dominated finite weights

Theorem 6.100 (Small remainder forces the greedy word). Let g≥1g\ge1 and let w1,…,wmw_1,\ldots,w_m be nonnegative integer weights satisfying wi≥g+∑j>iwj(1≤i≤m).w_i\ge g+\sum_{j>i}w_j\qquad(1\le i\le m). Fix an integer capacity C≥0C\ge0. The greedy word γ\gamma is obtained by taking wiw_i exactly when it does not exceed the remaining capacity. For an admissible Boolean word ε\varepsilon, meaning ∑iεiwi≤C\sum_i\varepsilon_iw_i\le C, one has C−∑iεiwi<g⇔ε=γandC−∑iγiwi<g.C-\sum_i\varepsilon_iw_i<g \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \varepsilon=\gamma\ \text{and}\ C-\sum_i\gamma_iw_i<g. Indeed, two different words have sums separated by at least gg, as seen at their first differing index; the greedy sum is the largest admissible sum. Thus there is at most one admissible word with remainder below gg, and any such word is greedy. The greedy word alone need not have remainder below gg: for weights (5)(5), gap g=2g=2 and capacity C=3C=3, its remainder is 33.

Obstructions and countermodels

The results below test particular proposed implications. A countermodel to an abstract transition rule shows that the rule needs an additional hypothesis; it does not disprove a more structured arithmetic argument. Each entry states the information retained by its model and the conclusion that this information fails to imply.

Theorem 6.127 (A bounded model of the doubling-or-return alternative). The dichotomy ExactLocalMersenneHalfRow(2n−1)∨∃c,4≤c≤n∧ExactLocalMersenneHalfRow(2c−2)\mathrm{ExactLocalMersenneHalfRow}(2n{-}1) \vee \exists c,\,4\le c\le n\wedge \mathrm{ExactLocalMersenneHalfRow}(2c{-}2) (proved for n≥6n\ge6 at Theorem 6.128 below) is not by itself enough for cofinality. Countermodel: boundedDoubleOrRecycleModel(n):=(n=6)\mathrm{boundedDoubleOrRecycleModel}(n) := (n=6) satisfies exactly the same two-branch transition shape (seed at 6, and boundedDoubleOrRecycleModel_transition reproduces the ∨\vee shape by always taking the recycle branch with c=4c=4, conclusion back at 2⋅4−2=62\cdot4-2=6), yet ¬(∀N,∃n≥N,boundedDoubleOrRecycleModel(n))(not cofinal ; only ever true at n=6).\neg\big(\forall N,\ \exists n\ge N,\ \mathrm{boundedDoubleOrRecycleModel}(n)\big) \qquad \text{(not cofinal ; only ever true at } n=6\text{)}. Packaged existentially as exists_seeded_bounded_double_or_recycle_model. The double-or-recycle transition shape, even together with an endpoint-six seed, is logically insufficient to conclude cofinal exact rows. A genuinely new progress input (strict endpoint growth, or an independent cofinality argument) is required. The countermodel retains only the seed and this transition rule. It therefore tests those premises, not additional arithmetic information that a more structured induction may use.

Five declarations extend the already-cited SeamMiddleProducerSqrtEscape hypothesis with a reduction in the cases that remain to be checked, using the proved exclusion of the −3-3 cell. No strict separation of the existence conditions is inferred from dropping that case.

The finite-horizon condition can be stated without a separate private predicate. Recall the integer margin Fk(J)F_k(J) from Theorem 6.13 and the equivalence in .

Rewriting the signed carry recurrence

Numeral-adjacent boundary words have more structure than the previously used coefficient bound. If the lower suffix numeral is one larger than the upper suffix numeral, there is a unique carry pivot dd: rank dd enters the lower support, every rank ee with d<e≤Nd<e\le N flips from lower-unselected to upper-selected, and all ranks below dd agree (, [Lean], (uniform), support rigidity, half-carry recurrence). Hence for every positive coefficient row m≥1m\ge1 the boundary discrepancy is the exact divisor-incidence identity clow(m)+#{e:d<e≤N,e∣m}=cup(m)+𝟏d∣m,c_\mathrm{low}(m)+\#\{e:d<e\le N,\ e\mid m\} =c_\mathrm{up}(m)+\mathbf 1_{d\mid m}, not merely an inequality (, [Lean]).

The stage-level theorem consumes adjacent profiled prefixes directly (, [Lean]). This is a local normal form for the two-sheet boundary. It does not produce adjacent stages cofinally and therefore does not close HALF or universal #257.

This short module restates U257\mathrm{U257} in the new namespace () and gives it a problem-centric interface to the legacy half-terminal required input already used for O2 above: any finite supports with vanishing scaled terminal carry witness gives an infinite AA with XA(2)=1/2X_{A}(2)=1/2 (, [Lean]), hence refutes U257\mathrm{U257} outright (, [Lean]). Integer-quotient tests for one twenty-first

The later quotient-greedy analysis removes the diffuse alternatives. Let TwentyOneFatalAlignedBranch denote the explicit branch consisting of a fatal greedy gap, finite skipped support (hence cofinite selection), eventual alignment between the quotient rows and the rational greedy prefix, and eventual visits to every doubling block. Then 121∈𝒜⇔¬𝚃𝚠𝚎𝚗𝚝𝚢𝙾𝚗𝚎𝙵𝚊𝚝𝚊𝚕𝙰𝚕𝚒𝚐𝚗𝚎𝚍𝙱𝚛𝚊𝚗𝚌𝚑.\frac1{21}\in\ensuremath{\mathcal A} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \neg\,\mathtt{TwentyOneFatalAlignedBranch}. greedy recurrence.

On the fatal branch the canonical quotient remainder sRs_R is eventually strictly above the closed capacity 2R2^R (), and thereafter the support appends R+1R+1 while sRs_R follows one explicit affine recurrence (). Conversely, closed rows sR≤2Rs_R\le2^R along any unbounded sequence decay after normalisation and put 1/211/21 in the achievement set (; ).

This is the exact current contribution: membership has been reduced to excluding one named permanent affine-supercapacity regime. No theorem excludes that regime, forces unbounded closed returns, or proves membership. Combined with the finite-support obstruction above, membership would provide an infinite-support rational counterexample to universal #257; its present status remains [Open].

IV. Scales, conditional interfaces and unresolved inputs

Finite ranges and unbounded parameters

Every claim in this programme carries a scale tag alongside its evidence band. The two axes are independent and both matter to a reader deciding whether a result can be used as a premise. Evidence labels record the type of support supplied with a claim. [Lean] refers to the cited formal source and its recorded build status, not a new kernel run in this revision. A newly cited release file marked release_only in the packet is described as [Lean source]; that label does not promote it to the packet’s checked-build class. [Cert] denotes an exact finite computation; the surrounding text distinguishes fresh checks from inherited reports. [Math] denotes an ordinary mathematical argument, not independent human certification. [Cited] invokes the stated external result, and [Open] marks an unproved hypothesis.

The scale records the quantified range. A (fixed) claim concerns a specified value; (bounded) denotes either a finite tested range or a witness bounded in terms of the input. A (uniform) assertion applies to every index in its stated range, with its hypotheses retained; it need not be unconditional. A (cofinal) assertion has the form ∀N∃n≥N,P(n)\forall N\,\exists n\ge N,\ P(n). Compatibility between its witnesses is an additional requirement only when explicitly imposed. Definitions and scale-free statements are marked (n/a).

The important distinction is between obtaining a witness in a finite range and proving the quantified assertion used by a membership test. For example, half-membership follows from unbounded successful exact rows or from infinitely many greedy skips. A different sufficient condition asks for a bound at every reset beyond its threshold. These statements have different quantifiers, even when the same transition formulas occur in their proofs. Each row must retain its predicate, quantified variable, and every premise. An unconditional eventual assertion ∀n≥N0,P(n)\forall n\ge N_0,\,P(n) does give cofinal witnesses to that same predicate, by taking n=max⁡(N,N0)n=\max(N,N_0). A uniform conditional implication H(n)⇒C(n)H(n)\Rightarrow C(n) supplies no witness until H(n)H(n) is established, and a checked finite band supplies no assertion beyond its endpoints. These are different logical shapes and are recorded separately below.

Table [tab:scale-ladder] separates established finite or quantified results from unproved membership hypotheses and the proved implications that use them. Its lower part therefore contains proved theorems as well as open assumptions. The scale alone determines neither evidence nor truth status; the stated predicate and premises do.

Quantifiers and evidence for the stated results. The labels separate finite tests, uniform implications, unbounded witness conditions and all-reset hypotheses. A theorem conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not a proof of that hypothesis.

Remark 7.1 (Finite checks and quantified conclusions). The supplied audit examined eighteen possible implications from recorded results to the required unbounded-witness conditions. It reported no such implication. This is a report about those attempts, not a theorem excluding other arguments and not a fresh kernel replay.

For example, checks reset indices 1313 through 3030; it has no conclusion beyond that range. Likewise, a bound depending on the depth need not produce a witness at a larger depth. Conversely, a proved eventual assertion of the same witness predicate immediately gives cofinal witnesses. The issue is the precise premise and conclusion, not the name of its scale or the tactic used in a finite proof.

Approximations to the greedy orbit

Four reported calculations

Fix the weights xn:=1/(2n−1)x_n:=1/(2^n-1), n≥2n\ge2, and the target 1/21/2. The single object under study throughout this programme is the greedy orbit for this target: a residual ρ\rho starts at 1/21/2, and at rank kk the orbit takes iff ρ≥xk\rho\ge x_k. A skip at rank kk is safe iff ρ≤Tk+1:=∑j>kxj\rho\le T_{k+1}:=\sum_{j>k}x_j and fatal iff ρ∈(Tk+1,xk)\rho\in(T_{k+1},x_k) ; the fatal interval is exactly the gap no later tail can repair. The four calculations below concern this target, but their finite parameters and certification records differ. Agreement with the real greedy prefix requires a convergence argument for the approximants used in each calculation; agreement over a tested range is not that argument.

  • Truncation rung JJ. Replace the full weight xnx_n by the JJ-term truncation wn(J):=∑q=1J2−qnw_n^{(J)}:=\sum_{q=1}^{J}2^{-qn} and ask whether some Boolean support hits 1/21/2 exactly under the truncated weights. Certified for 3≤J≤223\le J\le22 (Table [tab:scale-ladder], bounded row; Theorem 8.6–8.9 below).

  • Seam row ss. The base-4 seam recursion tracking the deviation Δs:=rem(s)−2s\Delta_s:=\mathrm{rem}(s)-2^s of the integer greedy orbit from its dyadic target.   • Sharp tail margin. The rank-by-rank take/skip margin against the exact tail, checked for ranks 22 through 30003000: 14971497 takes against 15021502 skips, zero fatal skips anywhere, minimum safe-skip margin +2.9922+2.9922 bits at rank 55, and the smallest reported take-margin +0.0340+0.0340 bits at rank 77, where the remainder 1/1261/126 exceeds the weight 1/1271/127. Proposition 8.1 (Stability of each fixed greedy prefix). Let tj→1/2t_j\to1/2 and, for each fixed n≥2n\ge2, let vn(j)→xn=(2n−1)−1v_n^{(j)}\to x_n=(2^n-1)^{-1}, with vn(j)>0v_n^{(j)}>0. Apply the greedy rule with target tjt_j and weights vn(j)v_n^{(j)} in increasing order of nn, through depths mj→∞m_j\to\infty. For every fixed depth KK, the decisions at ranks 2,…,K2,\ldots,K eventually agree with those of the real half-greedy rule. This assertion concerns finite prefixes, not survival at all ranks.

Lean: paper_one_orbit_stability, approx_orbit_induction, tailGreedyRemainder_mersenne.

Proof. At rank 22, the target and the weight converge to their real counterparts. Their comparison is strict by Lemma 8.2, so its sign is eventually unchanged. Inductively, once all earlier decisions agree, the approximate remainder is the target minus a fixed finite sum of convergent weights. It therefore converges to the real remainder. The next comparison is again strict, so the next decision eventually agrees. A finite induction through KK proves the claim. ◻

Lemma 8.2 (No-ties lemma). At every rank kk of the full greedy orbit for target 1/21/2, both defining comparisons are strict: ρ≠xk\rho\ne x_k and ρ≠Tk+1\rho\ne T_{k+1}.

Lean: paper_no_ties, paper_no_ties_take, paper_no_ties_skip, irrational_mersenneTail.

Proof. The two strict comparisons have different reasons: parity excludes equality with a weight, and irrationality excludes equality with the complete tail.

Take boundary excluded (parity). Write a finite Mersenne sum as p/q=∑d∈Fxdp/q=\sum_{d\in F}x_d in lowest terms. Its denominator qq is odd, because every 2d−12^d-1 is odd (equivalently, , itself traced to ). Hence the residual after any finite prefix is ρ=12−pq=q−2p2q\rho=\tfrac12-\tfrac pq=\tfrac{q-2p}{2q}: its reduced denominator is even. Every weight xk=1/(2k−1)x_k=1/(2^k-1) has odd denominator. An even-denominator rational can never equal an odd-denominator rational, so ρ=xk\rho=x_k is impossible at any rank ; the take comparison is never a tie.

Skip-safety boundary excluded (irrationality). The tail past rank kk is Tk+1=E−1−∑2≤j≤kxjT_{k+1}=E-1-\sum_{2\le j\le k}x_j, where E=∑n≥11/(2n−1)E=\sum_{n\ge1}1/(2^n-1) is the Erdős–Borwein constant: a rational shift of EE. Erdős’s own 1948 theorem gives EE irrational (, instantiated at b=2b=2), so Tk+1T_{k+1} is irrational for every kk. The residual ρ\rho arising from any finite Boolean prefix is rational. An irrational number never equals a rational one, so ρ=Tk+1\rho=T_{k+1} is impossible at any rank ; the skip-safety comparison is never a tie either.

Both boundaries of the fatal interval (Tk+1,xk)(T_{k+1},x_k) are therefore approached only strictly, at every rank, unconditionally. ◻

Remark 8.3. The hypotheses of Proposition 8.1 can be checked for two concrete approximations. The truncated geometric weights ∑q=1J2−qn\sum_{q=1}^{J}2^{-qn} increase to xnx_n. For the integer quotient rows, division by 4s4^s gives weights 4−s⌊4s/(2n−1)⌋→xn4^{-s}\lfloor4^s/(2^n-1)\rfloor\to x_n and target 4−s(22s−1−2s)=1/2−2−s→1/24^{-s}(2^{2s-1}-2^s)=1/2-2^{-s}\to1/2. Hence both greedy rules agree with each fixed real prefix once their parameters are large enough. Convergent upper and lower bounds for RkR_k likewise determine the strict tail comparison at a fixed rank. No conclusion about the advisory margin scan follows without specifying its approximants and proving their convergence. Fixed-prefix agreement is not uniform agreement through a growing depth. For the quotient rows, however, summability bounds the unmatched tail by RKR_K and does give convergence of the coded values, as proved in Theorem 6.2. It identifies their limit as XG(2)X_G(2); it does not establish that this value is 1/21/2.

Theorem 8.9 (Finite decision procedure). Call n∈[4,LJ/2]n\in[4,L_J/2] bad if no M∈[n,2n−2]M\in[n,2n-2] has μJ(M)≤1115\mu_J(M)\le\tfrac{11}{15}, and set B(J):=max⁡(bad∪{3})B(J):=\max(\mathrm{bad}\cup\{3\}). Then HalfRung(J)\mathrm{HalfRung}(J) holds iff the greedy orbit for 1/21/2 under weights wn(J)w_n^{(J)} survives every rank from 22 through B(J)B(J). This is a finite exact decision procedure.

Proof. Survival at all ranks plainly implies survival through B(J)B(J). If AA represents 1/21/2 with the JJ-truncated weights, then 0≤XA(2)−12≤∑q>J2−2q1−2−q≤2∑q>J4−q=234−J.0\le X_A(2)-\tfrac12 \le\sum_{q>J}\frac{2^{-2q}}{1-2^{-q}} \le2\sum_{q>J}4^{-q}=\frac23\,4^{-J}. Consequently, such representations for an unbounded sequence of JJ would put 1/21/2 in the closed set 𝒜\mathcal A. Its representing support would be infinite, since finite Mersenne sums have odd denominator (Lemma 8.2); Lemma 8.5 separately excludes finite support for each truncation. The unbounded-index assertion is still unproved. Twenty verified values of JJ do not establish it.

Which hypotheses remain unproved

This section compares the stated results with the remaining hypotheses. Parts I–II assembled the corpus; here every result in it is tested against three exact open obligations and rendered as a usable premise: what it yields, the exact mismatch against the obligation, a classified gap kind (hypothesis_strength, a different parameter range, quantifier_order, a different expression of the same condition, or multiple), and the exact auxiliary statement that would close it. Nothing here decides #249 or #257; the corpus’s own moderator standard applies throughout: a conditional reduction is a result with a hypothesis, not a proof of that hypothesis, and a finite verified list is not a cofinal supply.

The three #257 obligations, stated exactly

Definition 9.1 (257-reset). For every upper or middle reset row r≥10r\ge10, require Δr+12>2r+5\Delta_{r+1}^2>2^{r+5}, where Δr+1=rem(r+1)−2r+1\Delta_{r+1}=\mathrm{rem}(r+1)-2^{r+1}. The finite range 10≤r<3110\le r<31 must be covered as well as the tail. Section 12.5 gives the exact conditional implication from this hypothesis. A proposed bound on right-run lengths is a different statement until the pulse corrections and endpoint conventions are matched. Finite observations establish neither failure of every constant run bound nor logarithmic asymptotic growth.

Definition 9.2 (257-cofinal-rows). ∀N∃n≥N\forall N\ \exists n \ge N with nn ; i.e. cofinally many finite prefixes whose local Mersenne quotient lands exactly on the half-value residue class. Consumed unconditionally by . No coherence between the witnessing rows is demanded and none should be assumed: the rows may be, and in the corpus’s own words, mutually incompatible ; only their endpoint lengths need tend to infinity. Requiring compatibility would add a condition on the witnesses. Whether that condition can be obtained from this existence statement needs a separate extraction argument; it is not a strict logical comparison merely because the witnesses are described differently.

Definition 9.3 (257-universal). The original question is the base-22 statement: ∑n∈A(2n−1)−1\sum_{n\in A}(2^n-1)^{-1} is irrational for every infinite A⊆ℕ≥1A\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}. Asking the same for every integer base b≥2b\ge2 is a stronger all-base extension, not the definition of Problem #257 itself.

Reading a row

Each entry identifies the available result, the assumptions needed to apply it, and the further estimate still required. A source link supports the stated declaration, not every proposed consequence in the discussion. Ordinary deductions and finite computations are identified separately.

Observation 9.34 (Rational targets and infinitely many greedy skips). [Lean] (forward ; reverse ). For every rational x≥0x\ge0, x∈𝒜⇔the greedy algorithm for x skips infinitely many ranks.x\in\mathcal A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{the greedy algorithm for $x$ skips infinitely many ranks}. The reverse implication holds for every real x≥0x\ge0: a fatal remainder rn(x)>Rnr_n(x)>R_n forces every subsequent weight to be taken, because Rn=wn+1+Rn+1R_n=w_{n+1}+R_{n+1}. Hence infinitely many skips exclude a fatal remainder, and Theorem 1.10 gives membership. For the forward implication, membership identifies the greedy sum with xx. Finitely many skips would make that sum EE minus a finite rational sum, which is irrational by Erdős’s theorem [1]. This contradicts rationality of xx and proves the stated extension as an ordinary argument.

Infinitely many skips do not mean infinitely many selected ranks: x=1/3x=1/3 has the single-element support {2}\{2\} and skips every other rank. Thus the equivalence does not decide which rational targets are represented, or provide an infinite support with rational value. The supplied half-target declarations remain identified above; a new target-uniform Lean theorem is not claimed. [Math]

Finite symmetric difference preserves eventual periodicity. Thus the finite-perturbation argument alone cannot extend this theorem to an aperiodic tail; a further hypothesis or argument is needed.

Three combined conditional arguments

The first conditional implication also appears in the supplied release source, as identified below. The other two entries are ordinary mathematical arguments about what the stated hypotheses would imply. None establishes its unproved orbit hypothesis or decides #257.

Theorem 9.46 (A: a sufficient lower bound at every reset). Assume that |rem(r+1)−2r+1|>2(r+5)/2|\mathrm{rem}(r+1)-2^{r+1}|>2^{(r+5)/2} for every upper or middle reset r≥10r\ge10. Then 1/2∈𝒜1/2\in\mathcal A.

The supplied release source states this implication as Lean source. The packet classifies that file as release_only; its proof body was inspected for this exposition, without a new kernel replay. Here is the role of the constants. Put B(r)=2⌊(r+4)/2⌋+2r+3.B(r)=2^{\lfloor(r+4)/2\rfloor}+2r+3. For r≥10r\ge10, the source proves B(r)2≤2r+5B(r)^2\le2^{r+5}. A right branch at the first crossing of the largest omitted rank rr would force |Δr+1|≤B(r)|\Delta_{r+1}|\le B(r), by tracing the exact affine recurrence back to that reset. The assumed strict lower bound excludes this crossing. The largest-skip induction then gives half-membership. The hypothesis concerns every actual reset beyond the threshold; neither a long finite check nor an asserted run-length asymptotic supplies it.
